items.title: I can define typical and atypical behaviour and distinguish between them
items.what: Typical behaviour is activity that is consistent with how an individual usually behaves. Atypical behaviour is activity that is unusual or unnatural compared to how that same individual usually behaves.
items.why: The distinction is always individual-centred, not society-centred. A behaviour that is unusual for the general population can still be typical for a specific person, and vice versa.
items.example: A professional swimmer spending four hours in a pool daily is typical for them, even though most people never swim for that long. If they suddenly stopped swimming entirely, that absence of usual behaviour would be atypical for them.

subtopic.name: Categorising Typical and Atypical Behaviour
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces the concepts of typical and atypical behaviour and explains the five psychological criteria used to categorise them: cultural perspectives, social norms, statistical rarity, personal distress, and maladaptive behaviour. The focus is always on the individual and how their behaviour compares to how they usually act.
subtopic.why: Psychologists need a shared framework for deciding whether a behaviour warrants concern or intervention. Without clear criteria, judgements about behaviour risk being arbitrary, culturally biased, or unfair to the individual being assessed.

items.title: I can explain how cultural perspectives are used as a psychological criterion
items.what: Cultural perspectives refers to the influence of society and community on one's thoughts, including awareness of different customs, beliefs, traditions, etiquette, and attitudes toward mental health. When applying this criterion, a behaviour is assessed against what is considered normal within the individual's cultural background.
items.why: A behaviour that appears unusual in one culture may be entirely ordinary in another. Ignoring cultural context risks mislabelling normal cultural practices as atypical or disordered.
items.example: In Japan, avoiding direct eye contact is a sign of respect. In Australia, the same behaviour might be read as evasive or socially awkward. A Japanese person avoiding eye contact in Australia is behaving typically for their cultural background, even if it appears atypical by local norms.

subtopic.why: Psychologists need a shared framework for deciding whether a behaviour warrants concern or intervention. Without clear criteria, judgements about behaviour risk being arbitrary, culturally biased, or unfair to the individual being assessed.

items.title: I can explain how social norms are used as a psychological criterion
items.what: Social norms are society's unofficial rules and expectations about how individuals should behave. They exist on a broader scale than cultural perspectives and can shift over time. A behaviour is assessed against what is generally expected of people in a given social context.
items.why: Social norms provide a practical baseline for identifying when someone's behaviour diverges significantly from what is expected in their social environment, which can signal that something has changed for that individual.
items.example: It is a social norm for students to sit quietly and complete work in class. A student who is constantly jumping around while all peers are seated and working is behaving in a way that clearly deviates from that norm, making the behaviour easy to identify as atypical.

subtopic.why: Psychologists need a shared framework for deciding whether a behaviour warrants concern or intervention. Without clear criteria, judgements about behaviour risk being arbitrary, culturally biased, or unfair to the individual being assessed.

items.title: I can explain how statistical rarity is used as a psychological criterion
items.what: Statistical rarity refers to a behaviour or characteristic that lies outside the range of statistical normality and is unusual enough to be considered significant. If only a small percentage of people exhibit a behaviour, it is statistically rare and therefore potentially atypical.
items.why: Statistical rarity provides an objective, measurable way to categorise behaviour that reduces reliance on subjective judgement. It allows comparisons across groups rather than relying solely on individual history.
items.example: An IQ of 160 is held by approximately 0.003% of the population, making it a statistical rarity. Similarly, if only 1 student in a class of 30 scores above 55 out of 60 on a test, that score is statistically rare compared to the group's results.

The focus is always on the individual and how their behaviour compares to how they usually act.
subtopic.why: Psychologists need a shared framework for deciding whether a behaviour warrants concern or intervention. Without clear criteria, judgements about behaviour risk being arbitrary, culturally biased, or unfair to the individual being assessed.

items.title: I can explain how personal distress is used as a psychological criterion
items.what: Personal distress is an aversive and often self-oriented emotional reaction that is inconsistent with how the individual usually feels or behaves. It does not have to be visible; distress can be internalised and difficult for others to detect.
items.why: Personal distress signals that something has changed for an individual at an emotional level, even when external behaviour appears unchanged. It is especially useful when cultural and statistical criteria are not applicable.
items.example: A student who is normally a confident public speaker but suddenly has shaking hands and a trembling voice before a presentation is displaying personal distress. The change from their usual state indicates atypical behaviour, even if their overall presentation still appears competent to observers.

subtopic.name: Categorising Typical and Atypical Behaviour
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces the concepts of typical and atypical behaviour and explains the five psychological criteria used to categorise them: cultural perspectives, social norms, statistical rarity, personal distress, and maladaptive behaviour. The focus is always on the individual and how their behaviour compares to how they usually act.
subtopic.why: Psychologists need a shared framework for deciding whether a behaviour warrants concern or intervention. Without clear criteria, judgements about behaviour risk being arbitrary, culturally biased, or unfair to the individual being assessed.

items.title: I can explain how maladaptive behaviour is used as a psychological criterion
items.what: Maladaptive behaviour is an action that impairs an individual's ability to meet the changing demands of their everyday life. It is a more outward indicator of atypicality than personal distress and focuses on whether the person can function effectively.
items.why: Maladaptive behaviour shows that a person is not just feeling differently but is actually unable to cope with or adapt to their normal environment. This has practical consequences for their daily functioning, relationships, and responsibilities.
items.example: Staying in bed for one day after a relationship break-up is not maladaptive, as it serves a coping function. However, remaining in bed for three weeks and missing school or work would be maladaptive, because it prevents the person from meeting their usual daily demands.

subtopic.name: Categorising Typical and Atypical Behaviour
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces the concepts of typical and atypical behaviour and explains the five psychological criteria used to categorise them: cultural perspectives, social norms, statistical rarity, personal distress, and maladaptive behaviour. The focus is always on the individual and how their behaviour compares to how they usually act.
subtopic.why: Psychologists need a shared framework for deciding whether a behaviour warrants concern or intervention. Without clear criteria, judgements about behaviour risk being arbitrary, culturally biased, or unfair to the individual being assessed.

items.title: I can explain the difference between maladaptive and atypical behaviour and why they are not synonyms
items.what: Atypical behaviour means acting in a way that is unusual for the individual. Maladaptive behaviour means acting in a way that hinders the ability to adjust to one's environment and function effectively. A behaviour can be atypical without being maladaptive, but maladaptive behaviour usually also indicates atypicality.
items.why: Conflating these two concepts leads to inaccurate assessments. A teenager becoming more defiant of parental rules is atypical compared to their childhood behaviour, but may be a normal and adaptive part of adolescent development rather than a cause for concern.
items.example: A child who was very obedient at age seven but begins pushing boundaries at age fourteen is behaving atypically relative to their earlier self. However, if this boundary-testing is developmentally normal for adolescence and does not prevent them from going to school or maintaining friendships, it is not maladaptive.

The focus is always on the individual and how their behaviour compares to how they usually act.
subtopic.why: Psychologists need a shared framework for deciding whether a behaviour warrants concern or intervention. Without clear criteria, judgements about behaviour risk being arbitrary, culturally biased, or unfair to the individual being assessed.

items.title: I can evaluate the usefulness and limitations of cultural perspectives as a criterion
items.what: Cultural perspectives are useful because they allow different cultural contexts to be taken into account and support collective evaluation of behaviour. The limitation is that in multicultural societies, multiple cultural norms intersect, making it difficult to isolate which cultural influences are relevant.
items.why: A criterion that ignores culture risks pathologising normal cultural practices. However, in diverse societies, it becomes harder to determine which cultural framework should apply to a given individual, reducing the criterion's precision.
items.example: A psychologist working with a client from a culture where emotional restraint is valued might correctly recognise that not expressing distress openly is culturally typical. But in a multicultural city where the client has lived across multiple cultural contexts, it may be unclear which cultural norm best applies to their behaviour.

subtopic.name: Evaluating Psychological Criteria
subtopic.what: This subtopic focuses on the strengths and limitations of each of the five psychological criteria used to categorise behaviour as typical or atypical. Understanding both sides of each criterion allows for more accurate and fair assessments of behaviour.
subtopic.why: No single criterion provides a complete picture. Each has contexts in which it works well and contexts in which it fails or misleads. Knowing these limitations prevents over-reliance on any one measure and supports more nuanced clinical judgement.

items.title: I can evaluate the usefulness and limitations of social norms as a criterion
items.what: Social norms are useful because they provide a clear baseline for comparison, making atypical behaviour relatively easy to identify. The limitation is that social norms are context-dependent, so the same behaviour may be typical in one setting and atypical in another, requiring additional effort to assess accurately.
items.why: Baselines simplify identification of divergence. But a criterion that shifts depending on context demands more interpretive work and risks producing inconsistent conclusions if context is not carefully considered.
items.example: Cheering loudly is typical at a football game but atypical during a formal debate. A psychologist assessing someone who cheers during a debate must account for context before concluding the behaviour is atypical, rather than simply applying a general social norm.

subtopic.name: Evaluating Psychological Criteria
subtopic.what: This subtopic focuses on the strengths and limitations of each of the five psychological criteria used to categorise behaviour as typical or atypical. Understanding both sides of each criterion allows for more accurate and fair assessments of behaviour.
subtopic.why: No single criterion provides a complete picture. Each has contexts in which it works well and contexts in which it fails or misleads. Knowing these limitations prevents over-reliance on any one measure and supports more nuanced clinical judgement.

items.title: I can evaluate the usefulness and limitations of statistical rarity as a criterion
items.what: Statistical rarity is useful because it provides an objective, measurable way to categorise behaviour that reduces subjective bias. The limitations are that not all statistical rarities indicate harm or dysfunction, and it can be difficult to apply percentages to abstract or variable human behaviours.
items.why: Objectivity is valuable in psychological assessment, but objectivity alone does not determine whether a behaviour is problematic. A statistically rare behaviour may be highly positive, neutral, or harmful, and numbers cannot always capture the nuance of individual behaviour.
items.example: Scoring in the top 0.1% on a mathematics test is a statistical rarity, but it is not a sign of atypicality in any concerning sense. Conversely, attempting to quantify what percentage of people feel a certain emotion on a given day is difficult because emotional expressions vary enormously between individuals.

subtopic.name: Evaluating Psychological Criteria
subtopic.what: This subtopic focuses on the strengths and limitations of each of the five psychological criteria used to categorise behaviour as typical or atypical. Understanding both sides of each criterion allows for more accurate and fair assessments of behaviour.
subtopic.why: No single criterion provides a complete picture. Each has contexts in which it works well and contexts in which it fails or misleads. Knowing these limitations prevents over-reliance on any one measure and supports more nuanced clinical judgement.

items.title: I can evaluate the usefulness and limitations of personal distress as a criterion
items.what: Personal distress is useful when cultural, statistical, and social criteria are not applicable, and it can provide visible evidence that a person is behaving differently from their norm. The limitation is that many individuals conceal or suppress distress, making it hard for others to detect and therefore hard to use as a reliable indicator.
items.why: Distress is a meaningful signal of change, but it relies on some degree of observable or reportable evidence. When individuals mask their distress, the criterion becomes unreliable and may result in underidentification of atypical behaviour.
items.example: A person who is usually calm and talkative suddenly becomes quiet and tearful in social situations. The visible distress makes it straightforward to identify atypical behaviour. However, a different person experiencing the same internal state but choosing to appear composed would be harder to identify using this criterion alone.

subtopic.name: Evaluating Psychological Criteria
subtopic.what: This subtopic focuses on the strengths and limitations of each of the five psychological criteria used to categorise behaviour as typical or atypical. Understanding both sides of each criterion allows for more accurate and fair assessments of behaviour.
subtopic.why: No single criterion provides a complete picture. Each has contexts in which it works well and contexts in which it fails or misleads. Knowing these limitations prevents over-reliance on any one measure and supports more nuanced clinical judgement.

items.title: I can evaluate the usefulness and limitations of maladaptive behaviour as a criterion
items.what: Maladaptive behaviour is useful because it focuses on the consequences of behaviour, allowing the assessor to consider whether what appears problematic is actually harmful to functioning. The limitation is that judgements about what counts as maladaptive are subjective and can vary depending on who is making the assessment.
items.why: Focusing on functional consequences grounds assessment in real-world impact rather than appearance alone. However, subjectivity in defining 'effective functioning' means two assessors could reach different conclusions about the same behaviour.
items.example: One person might see a student avoiding conversation before an exam as maladaptive avoidance, while another might see it as a useful calming strategy. The same behaviour receives opposite categorisations depending on the assessor's interpretation of what counts as adaptive coping.

items.title: I can define normality and abnormality in a psychological context
items.what: Normality refers to the state of having thoughts, feelings, and behaviours that are considered common and acceptable. Abnormality is the state of deviating from the norm, usually in a way that is considered undesirable. Both concepts are subjective and context-dependent.
items.why: Having working definitions of normality and abnormality is necessary for psychological practice, but students must also understand that no single universal definition exists. The concept of normality is continuously evolving and can inadvertently stigmatise those labelled as 'abnormal'.
items.example: In the early twentieth century, left-handedness was frequently treated as abnormal and children were forced to write with their right hand. Today, left-handedness is understood as a normal variation, illustrating how the definition of normality changes over time.

subtopic.name: Normality and Neurotypicality
subtopic.what: This subtopic explores how normality is defined across six different approaches (socio-cultural, functional, historical, medical, statistical, and situational), and introduces the concept of neurotypicality as a way of describing individuals whose neurological and cognitive functioning follows an expected developmental trajectory.
subtopic.why: Normality is not a single fixed standard. Understanding the multiple frameworks used to define it helps explain why different people and professionals can reach different conclusions about the same behaviour, and why the concept of neurotypicality arose to help describe variation in brain functioning.

items.title: I can describe the six approaches to understanding normality
items.what: The six approaches are: socio-cultural (normality defined by social and cultural codes), functional (normality as the ability to cope with everyday demands), historical (normality changes across time periods), medical (abnormality has biological causes and clear symptoms), statistical (normality based on how the majority think and behave), and situational (normality varies by context).
items.why: Each approach captures a different dimension of what it means to be normal. Relying on only one produces an incomplete or distorted picture. Psychologists draw on multiple approaches when assessing an individual.
items.example: A person who hears voices might be considered abnormal under the medical approach (a diagnosable symptom), but within certain cultural or spiritual traditions the same experience could be considered a normal and meaningful phenomenon under the socio-cultural approach.

subtopic.name: Normality and Neurotypicality
subtopic.what: This subtopic explores how normality is defined across six different approaches (socio-cultural, functional, historical, medical, statistical, and situational), and introduces the concept of neurotypicality as a way of describing individuals whose neurological and cognitive functioning follows an expected developmental trajectory.
subtopic.why: Normality is not a single fixed standard. Understanding the multiple frameworks used to define it helps explain why different people and professionals can reach different conclusions about the same behaviour, and why the concept of neurotypicality arose to help describe variation in brain functioning.

items.title: I can define neurotypicality and identify common characteristics of neurotypical individuals
items.what: Neurotypicality describes individuals whose neurological and cognitive functioning is typical or expected, following a standard developmental trajectory and meeting recognised developmental milestones. Common characteristics include effective communication skills, similar social skills to peers, the ability to function in distracting environments without sensory overload, and the capacity to adapt to routine changes.
items.why: The term neurotypicality provides a reference point for understanding brain development. It exists in contrast to neurodiversity and helps clarify what is meant by expected cognitive and neurological functioning without implying that neurotypical individuals are superior.
items.example: According to developmental guidelines, smiling at people by two months, rolling from back to tummy by six months, and waving goodbye by twelve months are all behaviours considered typical for neurotypical infants. A child meeting these milestones on schedule would be described as neurotypical.

subtopic.what: This subtopic explores how normality is defined across six different approaches (socio-cultural, functional, historical, medical, statistical, and situational), and introduces the concept of neurotypicality as a way of describing individuals whose neurological and cognitive functioning follows an expected developmental trajectory.
subtopic.why: Normality is not a single fixed standard. Understanding the multiple frameworks used to define it helps explain why different people and professionals can reach different conclusions about the same behaviour, and why the concept of neurotypicality arose to help describe variation in brain functioning.

items.title: I can explain the origins of the term 'neurotypical' and its relationship to neurodiversity
items.what: The term neurotypical was coined by Australian sociologist Judy Singer in 1998 to refer to non-autistic individuals. It arose alongside the term neurodiversity, which emerged in the 1990s to reframe autism and related conditions as natural variations in brain functioning rather than deficits or disorders.
items.why: Understanding the historical and conceptual origins of these terms helps students use them accurately. The terms were developed to reduce stigma and create a more inclusive framework for understanding brain differences, not to separate people into fixed categories.
items.example: Before the neurodiversity framework, autism was often described primarily in terms of deficits and impairments. The introduction of the terms 'neurodivergent' and 'neurotypical' shifted the framing so that both ways of thinking are described as part of a continuum of normal brain functioning rather than as normal versus disordered.

Understanding the multiple frameworks used to define it helps explain why different people and professionals can reach different conclusions about the same behaviour, and why the concept of neurotypicality arose to help describe variation in brain functioning.

items.title: I can define adaptive and maladaptive and apply these terms to psychological development
items.what: Adaptive means being able to adjust to the environment appropriately and function effectively. Maladaptive means being unable to adapt to the environment appropriately and function effectively. Both terms relate to how well an individual can meet the changing demands of their life.
items.why: These terms provide a functional lens for assessing whether a person's psychological responses are helping or hindering them. They complement the typical/atypical distinction by focusing on consequences rather than just deviation from norms.
items.example: A child on their first day of school who gets their own lunchbox and eats independently is showing adaptive behaviour. A child who refuses to eat unless a teacher feeds them is showing maladaptive behaviour, because it prevents them from functioning independently in their new environment.

subtopic.name: Adaptive and Maladaptive Emotions, Behaviours and Cognitions
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines what it means to be adaptive or maladaptive across three domains of psychological development: emotions, behaviours, and cognitions. It also explores how adaptiveness is always assessed relative to age, developmental stage, and situational context.
subtopic.why: Adaptive functioning is closely linked to normality, but whether something is adaptive or maladaptive is not fixed. The same action can be adaptive in one context and maladaptive in another, and understanding this prevents oversimplified judgements about psychological development.

items.title: I can give examples of adaptive and maladaptive emotions
items.what: Adaptive emotions are those that are effectively regulated and displayed in a way that helps the individual cope with their circumstances. Maladaptive emotions are those that are poorly regulated or disproportionate in intensity or duration, hindering the individual's functioning.
items.why: Emotions such as sadness, worry, and fear are adaptive in many situations because they help people confront and manage threats. However, when these emotions persist for prolonged periods and begin to interfere with daily life, they become maladaptive and may indicate a mental health condition.
items.example: Feeling angry after being refused a new phone and calming down within a few hours using coping strategies is an adaptive emotional response. Staying intensely angry at a parent for a full month over the same event, to the point of refusing to speak to them or attend school, would be maladaptive.

subtopic.what: This subtopic examines what it means to be adaptive or maladaptive across three domains of psychological development: emotions, behaviours, and cognitions. It also explores how adaptiveness is always assessed relative to age, developmental stage, and situational context.

items.title: I can give examples of adaptive and maladaptive behaviours
items.what: Adaptive behaviours are activities that enhance an individual's ability to meet the changing demands of their everyday life. Maladaptive behaviours are activities that hinder this ability and prevent effective functioning.
items.why: Identifying whether a behaviour is adaptive or maladaptive helps determine whether intervention is warranted. A behaviour that appears concerning on the surface may actually be adaptive, and an apparently harmless behaviour may be quietly undermining a person's functioning.
items.example: Going for a social drink after work to unwind and connect with colleagues is an adaptive behaviour. Drinking to the point of being unable to function at work the following day is maladaptive, because it prevents the person from meeting their professional obligations.

subtopic.what: This subtopic examines what it means to be adaptive or maladaptive across three domains of psychological development: emotions, behaviours, and cognitions. It also explores how adaptiveness is always assessed relative to age, developmental stage, and situational context.

items.title: I can give examples of adaptive and maladaptive cognitions
items.what: Adaptive cognitions involve having awareness and knowledge that helps the individual adjust to different environments and situations. Maladaptive cognitions involve unhelpful thought patterns that make adjustment more difficult and distort interpretation of events.
items.why: Thought patterns directly influence emotional responses and behaviour. Maladaptive cognitions, such as catastrophising or overgeneralising, can drive a cycle of dysfunction even when external circumstances are manageable.
items.example: After failing a maths test, thinking 'this is feedback that I need to study differently' is an adaptive cognition that supports future improvement. Thinking 'I failed this test so I will never get a job' is a maladaptive cognition that is disproportionate to the evidence and likely to increase distress and reduce motivation.

items.title: I can explain why whether something is adaptive or maladaptive depends on age, context, and developmental stage
items.what: Adaptiveness is not fixed. The same behaviour can be adaptive at one age and maladaptive at another, and adaptive in one situation but maladaptive in another. Assessment must always consider the developmental stage and situational context of the individual.
items.why: Applying a single standard of adaptive behaviour across all ages and contexts produces inaccurate assessments. What is functional and expected for a toddler is not the same as what is functional and expected for a teenager or adult.
items.example: Crying and throwing a tantrum when lost in a supermarket is adaptive for a three-year-old, because crying is an effective way to attract an adult's attention in that situation. The same behaviour in a seventeen-year-old is maladaptive, because they have access to more effective strategies such as approaching a staff member or using a phone to call a guardian.

subtopic.why: Adaptive functioning is closely linked to normality, but whether something is adaptive or maladaptive is not fixed. The same action can be adaptive in one context and maladaptive in another, and understanding this prevents oversimplified judgements about psychological development.

items.title: I can explain why some apparently maladaptive behaviours may actually be adaptive for specific individuals
items.what: A behaviour that appears maladaptive in a general context may be adaptive for a particular individual based on their neurological profile, developmental history, or situational needs. Assessment must consider the function a behaviour serves for that specific person.
items.why: Applying a universal standard of adaptiveness without considering individual differences can lead to misclassification. A behaviour that disrupts others or appears non-functional may be serving an important regulatory or coping function for the individual.
items.example: A student rocking back and forth in a quiet classroom might appear maladaptive because it is disruptive and suggests they are not adjusting to the environment. However, for a student with autism, this behaviour (known as stimming) may be adaptive, as it helps them emotionally regulate and return to a functional state in an overstimulating environment.

items.title: I can define neurodiversity and neurodivergence and explain the relationship between them
items.what: Neurodiversity is the term used to describe variations in neurological development and functioning within and between groups of people. Neurodivergent refers to individuals who have a variation in neurological development and functioning, such as those diagnosed with ASD, ADHD, or dyslexia. Neurodiversity is the group-level concept; neurodivergent is the individual-level descriptor.
items.why: Precise use of these terms matters. Calling a group 'neurodiverse' and an individual 'neurodivergent' reflects the actual meaning of the terms and avoids inaccurate language. The framework was developed to normalise brain differences and reduce stigma.
items.example: A classroom that includes students with autism, ADHD, dyslexia, and no diagnosed condition has neurodiversity within it. An individual student diagnosed with dyslexia is described as neurodivergent. The classroom is neurodiverse; the student is neurodivergent.

subtopic.name: Neurodiversity
subtopic.what: This subtopic explores neurodiversity as an overarching concept describing normal variation in brain development, and examines three specific neurodivergent conditions in detail: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), and Dyslexia. For each condition, brain differences, strengths, challenges, prevalence, and management strategies are covered.
subtopic.why: Understanding neurodiversity allows students to recognise that variation in brain functioning is a normal feature of human populations, not a defect. It also builds the knowledge needed to support neurodivergent individuals appropriately in educational and professional contexts.

items.title: I can describe the key features, brain differences, strengths, and challenges of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)
items.what: ASD is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by impaired social interactions, verbal and non-verbal communication difficulties, narrow interests, and repetitive behaviours. Brain differences include a thinner temporal cortex, a thicker frontal cortex, smaller amygdala, and greater brain volume in childhood. Strengths include exceptional attention to detail and high motivation in areas of interest; challenges include difficulty reading facial expressions and distress over minor routine changes.
items.why: ASD presents differently across individuals and across genders, and understanding its neurological basis and functional profile helps students apply knowledge accurately to case study scenarios and real-world support contexts.
items.example: A person with ASD at a speed dating event might demonstrate the strength of superior retention of facts about a topic they are passionate about, sharing detailed knowledge about a specific country they have visited. At the same time, they might find it difficult to maintain eye contact, which is a recognised challenge associated with ASD.

items.title: I can describe the key features, brain differences, strengths, and challenges of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
items.what: ADHD is a neurological condition characterised by persistent inattention or hyperactivity that disrupts social, academic, or occupational functioning. Brain differences include delayed maturation of the cerebral cortex, smaller amygdala and hippocampus, and faster maturation of the motor cortex. Strengths include hyperfocus and creative problem-solving; challenges include time management, staying on topic, impulsivity, and difficulty articulating feelings.
items.why: ADHD is often mischaracterised as simply an inability to pay attention. Understanding hyperfocus and the neurological basis of the condition gives a more accurate picture and helps students avoid common misconceptions when applying the concept to scenarios.
items.example: A student with ADHD might spend three hours completely absorbed in building a detailed model, ignoring calls to dinner (hyperfocus, a strength), but the next morning be unable to spend ten minutes on a homework task they find uninteresting (difficulty sustaining attention on low-interest tasks, a challenge).

items.title: I can describe the key features, brain differences, strengths, and challenges of dyslexia
items.what: Dyslexia is a neurologically based learning difficulty involving severe challenges in reading, spelling, writing words, and sometimes arithmetic. Brain differences include decreased grey matter volume, weaker white matter organisation, hypoactivation of regions responsible for symbol-to-sound processing, and reduced neuroplasticity in left-hemispheric language areas. Strengths include strong memory, spatial awareness, and big-picture thinking; challenges include reading, writing, forming words, and lack of confidence in literacy-based tasks.
items.why: Dyslexia is frequently misunderstood as laziness or low intelligence. Understanding its neurological basis and the genuine strengths associated with it helps students assess scenarios accurately and avoid deficit-only framings of the condition.
items.example: A student with dyslexia might read 'hippocampus' and process it as 'hypothalamus' due to difficulty matching written symbols to sounds (a recognised challenge). The same student might be highly skilled at explaining complex psychological concepts through vivid verbal storytelling (narrative reasoning, a recognised strength).

subtopic.what: This subtopic explores neurodiversity as an overarching concept describing normal variation in brain development, and examines three specific neurodivergent conditions in detail: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), and Dyslexia. For each condition, brain differences, strengths, challenges, prevalence, and management strategies are covered.
subtopic.why: Understanding neurodiversity allows students to recognise that variation in brain functioning is a normal feature of human populations, not a defect. It also builds the knowledge needed to support neurodivergent individuals appropriately in educational and professional contexts.

items.title: I can compare ASD and ADHD in terms of similarities and differences
items.what: ASD and ADHD share some overlapping features, including repetitive behaviours and difficulty adapting to certain environments. However, ASD is primarily characterised by impaired social communication and narrow interests, whereas ADHD is primarily characterised by persistent inattention or hyperactivity. Brain structures differ between the two conditions, even when behavioural symptoms overlap.
items.why: Comorbidity between ASD and ADHD is documented, and the conditions share surface-level similarities that can lead to diagnostic confusion. Being able to distinguish between them is a key skill for applying psychological knowledge to case studies.
items.example: Both a person with ASD and a person with ADHD might engage in repetitive behaviour, but for different reasons. The person with ASD may repeat an action as part of a narrow, highly specific interest. The person with ADHD may repeat an action because of impulsivity or restlessness, not because of a focused interest.

items.title: I can identify management strategies for ASD, ADHD, and dyslexia
items.what: ASD can be managed through behavioural therapy, speech and occupational therapy, educational support, and medication for accompanying mental health conditions. ADHD can be managed through medication, counselling, and behavioural strategies such as decluttering, designating zones, using planners, and working in small increments. Dyslexia can be managed through audio or video learning, assistive text-to-speech technology, and occupational therapy.
items.why: Knowing management strategies is directly assessed in VCE Psychology and is relevant to real-world support contexts. Management is most effective when tailored to the individual's specific profile and implemented as early as possible.
items.example: A student with ADHD who struggles to focus during a maths lesson might benefit from their teacher implementing behavioural strategies: clearing their desk of unnecessary items (decluttering), working on one problem at a time with a short break after each (working in small increments), and using a visual planner to track which tasks have been completed.

items.title: I can describe the role, qualifications, and responsibilities of mental health workers
items.what: Mental health workers are members of a mental health treatment team who provide a wide range of services and care for people with psychological or social problems. They typically hold a bachelor's degree in nursing or social work and a mental health certification. They assist with medication management, coping strategy development, community connection, and support for families of people with disabilities or neurological conditions. They cannot diagnose mental illness or provide specific therapies.
items.why: Mental health workers form a critical support layer between clients and more highly credentialled professionals. Understanding their scope of practice prevents both underutilisation of their skills and unrealistic expectations of what they can do.
items.example: A mental health worker supporting a young adult with autism might help them connect with a local social group, review their recovery plan after they start a new job, and teach practical strategies for managing uncomfortable social situations. They would not diagnose the client or deliver formal cognitive behavioural therapy.

subtopic.name: Mental Health Workers, Psychologists, Psychiatrists and Organisations
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the qualifications, roles, and responsibilities of mental health workers, psychologists, and psychiatrists, as well as the services provided by mental health organisations. It also introduces culturally responsive practices as an essential dimension of all mental health work.
subtopic.why: Understanding who does what in the mental health system helps students identify the appropriate professional or service for a given scenario. It also highlights why culturally responsive practice is necessary for equitable and effective mental health support.

items.title: I can describe the role, qualifications, and responsibilities of psychologists
items.what: A psychologist is an individual professionally trained in one or more branches of psychology. Becoming a psychologist in Australia requires an accredited three-year undergraduate degree, a fourth year of honours, a master's degree in a specialisation, and formal registration with the Australian Psychological Society. Psychologists can diagnose mental health and developmental disorders, provide therapy (including cognitive behavioural therapy and psychoanalysis), refer clients to other specialists, and conduct research. They cannot prescribe medication.
items.why: Psychologists are often confused with psychiatrists. Knowing the precise scope and limits of a psychologist's role, particularly their inability to prescribe medication, is directly assessed in VCE and matters for accurately navigating case study scenarios.
items.example: A psychologist working with a student referred for distracted and inattentive classroom behaviour might assess the student, provide a diagnostic judgement about ADHD, develop a school support plan, and offer counselling. If the student requires medication, the psychologist would refer them to a psychiatrist.

items.title: I can describe the role, qualifications, and responsibilities of psychiatrists
items.what: A psychiatrist is a doctor who specialises in the diagnosis, treatment, prevention, and study of mental, behavioural, and personality disorders. Becoming a psychiatrist requires a medical degree (four to six years), one year of hospital training, and five years of specialist psychiatric training with the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists. Unlike psychologists, psychiatrists can prescribe medication. A referral from a GP or psychologist is required to see a psychiatrist.
items.why: The key distinction between psychologists and psychiatrists is the medical degree and prescribing authority. This distinction is directly and frequently tested in VCE Psychology and determines which professional pathway is appropriate for clients requiring medication.
items.example: A fourteen-year-old diagnosed with ADHD by a psychologist might be referred to a psychiatrist to discuss whether stimulant medication would be appropriate. The psychiatrist would also monitor for any side effects, manage any co-occurring conditions such as anxiety, and coordinate with the psychologist's support plan.

items.title: I can compare the roles of psychologists and psychiatrists and identify what is unique to each
items.what: Both psychologists and psychiatrists can diagnose mental health and developmental conditions, provide talk-based therapies, refer clients to other professionals, and develop management plans. Psychiatrists alone can prescribe medication, and their training is medical in nature rather than psychological. Psychologists typically have deeper training in therapeutic approaches and psychological assessment.
items.why: Exam questions frequently ask students to compare these two professions or identify why one would be more appropriate than the other in a given scenario. Knowing what they share and what distinguishes them is essential for accurate answers.
items.example: Sreya is a registered psychologist who cannot prescribe medication. When her parents ask her to diagnose and prescribe medication for a family friend's child with possible ADHD, she cannot do so: diagnosing is within her scope, but prescribing is not, as only a psychiatrist who holds a medical degree has that authority.

items.title: I can describe the role and services of mental health organisations and give examples
items.what: A mental health organisation is a company or group that works to address or advocate for mental health through support or specialised services. Services include raising awareness through brochures and flyers, school-based early intervention programs, over-the-phone counselling, and workshops teaching management strategies. Examples include Beyond Blue (anxiety, depression, suicide prevention) and Amaze (autism support).
items.why: Mental health organisations extend the reach of professional support into communities, particularly for people who cannot access or afford formal clinical services. Knowing the types of services they provide is directly assessed and practically useful.
items.example: Beyond Blue offers a 24/7 phone service, an online forum, informative fact sheets about anxiety and depression, and the Beyond Now app, which helps people create a personal suicide safety plan. A person experiencing heightened anxiety at 11pm who cannot reach their psychologist could access immediate support through Beyond Blue's phone line.

items.title: I can explain how mental health workers, psychologists, psychiatrists, and organisations work together to provide holistic support
items.what: These four types of support do not work in isolation. They form a coordinated network around a client, each contributing different services. For example, a psychiatrist might prescribe medication, a psychologist might provide therapy, a mental health worker might develop daily coping strategies, and an organisation might offer peer support groups or phone counselling.
items.why: Holistic care produces better outcomes than any single intervention. Understanding how these roles integrate also helps students answer extended response questions that ask them to plan or evaluate a comprehensive support structure for a client.
items.example: A person diagnosed with anxiety might receive medication from a psychiatrist to manage acute symptoms, cognitive behavioural therapy from a psychologist to address underlying thought patterns, daily coping strategy coaching from a mental health worker, and use Beyond Blue's phone line during high-anxiety moments outside business hours.

items.title: I can define culturally responsive practices and explain why they are important in mental health work
items.what: Culturally responsive practices involve acting in ways that respond to the needs of diverse communities and demonstrating openness to cultural ideas, beliefs, and values. Key skills include understanding different cultures, accepting differences without judgement, identifying cultural risk factors without stereotyping, and recognising one's own cultural biases.
items.why: Australia is a culturally diverse society. A mental health professional who fails to account for cultural background risks misdiagnosing typical cultural practices as atypical, or making clients feel unsafe and unacknowledged, which reduces the effectiveness and equity of care.
items.example: A psychologist working with a client from a culture where emotional restraint is valued should not interpret the client's reluctance to openly discuss their feelings as lack of insight or engagement. Instead, the psychologist should recognise this as a culturally typical response and adjust their approach, perhaps by working more slowly to build trust before expecting open emotional disclosure.
